core: The working definition of the trial balance: a list of all accounts in the general ledger with their balances at a point in time, used to check that total debits equal total credits (attributed to OpenStax's Principles of Accounting, with CFI's point-in-time framing)
How it works: each account's ending balance listed in two columns — debit balances on the left, credit balances on the right — with the columns totaled and compared
What a balanced trial balance means: debits equal credits, but it does not prove everything is right (the honest note)

What it cannot catch, each named: missing transactions (error of omission), wrong accounts (commission error), and equal mistakes on both sides (error of original entry), plus CFI's reversal and principle errors
The trial balance in the cycle: a step between the ledger and the statements (accounting-cycle is a sibling topic, referenced only)
When it is prepared: at the end of the accounting period, before the financial statements — unadjusted first, then adjusted after adjusting entries
The honest framing: the trial balance is a tripwire, not a verdict — it catches many errors, not all
supporting: The trial balance is an internal working document, not an official financial statement, and is usually not distributed outside the company (CFI Trial Balance)
Error-search methods for an unbalanced trial balance: divide the difference by two (wrong-column amounts) and by nine (transposed digits), then trace back step by step (OpenStax Section 3.6)
Formatting conventions: header with company name, trial-balance label, and date; accounts in accounting equation order (OpenStax Section 3.6)
The unadjusted trial balance is the fourth step of the accounting cycle; the adjusted trial balance is prepared after adjusting entries (OpenStax Section 3.6 and 3.3; CFI Accounting Cycle)

claims.claim: A trial balance is a list of all accounts in the general ledger with their balances at a point in time, used to check that total debits equal total credits.

The trial balance lists each account's ending balance in one of two columns — debit balances on the left, credit balances on the right — and the two columns are totaled; if the totals are not equal, there is a mistake in at least one of the columns.
A balanced trial balance (equal column totals) does not prove the books are correct; errors can still be present even when the columns match.

A trial balance cannot catch an error of omission (a transaction never entered), a commission error (the right amount in the wrong account), or an error of original entry (wrong amounts on both sides of an entry); CFI also lists reversal and principle errors as undetectable.

The trial balance is prepared at the end of the accounting period — monthly, quarterly, or yearly — after journal entries have been posted to the ledger and before the financial statements are prepared; it is the fourth step of the accounting cycle.
The unadjusted trial balance is prepared before adjusting entries; an adjusted trial balance is prepared after adjusting entries to confirm the totals still balance before the statements are built.
The trial balance is an internal working document, not an official financial statement, and is usually not distributed to people outside the company.

When a trial balance does not balance, standard search methods are to divide the difference by two (to find an amount in the wrong column) and to divide it by nine (to find transposed digits); if neither works, the bookkeeper traces back step by step from the trial balance to the ledger to the journal.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the trial balance lists every general ledger account or only accounts with nonzero balances.
positions: OpenStax's Principles of Accounting defines the trial balance as a list of all accounts in the general ledger that have nonzero balances
CFI describes it as a report that lists the balances of all general ledger accounts of a company at a certain point in time
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the common phrasing 'all accounts ... with their balances' and focuses on the essential idea — every account's ending balance, debit or credit, in one of two columns — which both sources support.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How many types of errors a balanced trial balance can hide.
positions: CFI names five undetectable error types: error of omission, error of original entry, error of reversal, principle error, and commission error
Simpler treatments commonly name three main classes: missing transactions, wrong accounts, and equal mistakes on both sides
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson names the three core classes in plain language (mapping to CFI's omission, commission, and original-entry errors) and mentions reversal and principle errors as additional cases, per CFI.
